notes: The .doc title page (opened as text): 'Ecological foot print and carrying capacity studies of South East Queensland: A comparison and discussion of results', Michael Gutteridge, 12 August 2005, commissioned by the Dept. of Natural Resources and Mines; the thesis (opened) cites it as a 2005 DNRM report. COMP's 'Gutteridge 2006' does not match the report's date; the slides file is named 2006 but its document properties show creation 2005-07-13 and last save 2009 and its text (opened) carries 'SEQ 2.6m (2005) and 3.7m (2026)'. The slides and tabulation workbook are supporting files from the same author, matched by author and subject, not by a title page of their own; the three sha256 values are in the order of the paths. B04 (2026-11-07): Settled: the 180,000-person carrying capacity is in the report (dated 12 August 2005) and in the slides. The "14 times" ratio does NOT appear in the report or in the slides (text searched); it is the thesis's own wording ("existing population of Southeast Queensland is 14 times over its resource-based carrying capacity", thesis PDF page 125). It matches the slides' "SEQ 2.6m (2005)" divided by 180,000 (14.4); the report uses 2,331,740 (NRM SEQ Draft Plan 2004), which gives 13.0, and 4 million by 2030 gives 22. what_taken: Integrated multi-model outlook (more than 20 scenarios, 2050) for the Australian National Outlook; pressures more than double, stabilise or fall markedly; decoupling possible but not automatic and needs no change in values; collective policy choices explain 46 to 94% of differences; carbon plantings 29 to 59 Mha in 2050 (up to 58 Mha, 70% of the intensive-use zone); no capacity figure.
notes: Full text of the article and Extended Data read from the archive copy; online Methods and Supplementary Information not held. Does not cite Lane in the printed references. L090 (the CSIRO report) stays not reached.

title: Bryan et al. 2016, Global Environmental Change 38: 130-152, "Land-use and sustainability under intersecting global change and domestic policy scenarios: Trajectories for Australia to 2050"
what_taken: LUTO partial-equilibrium land-use model, 648 scenarios, 85.3 Mha of intensive agricultural land, annual, about 1.1 km grid, 2013 to 2050; with strong global abatement incentives complemented by biodiversity-focussed domestic land-use policy, plantings and biofuels raise returns and ecosystem services without major impacts on agricultural production; crops and horticulture 89.5 to 162.7 Mt in 2050 (130.1 Mt under M3 Balanced) as grazing land falls up to 70%; 26 GB data pack; no capacity figure.
used_by: methods paper (section 4 (scenario model) and 6 (context: yield path, time frame, land taken by plantings))

title: Ridoutt et al. 2017, Food Security 9: 211-226, "Australia's nutritional food balance: situation, outlook and policy implications"
what_taken: Australian intake scenarios to 2050 (reported 2011 intake; Australian Guide to Healthy Eating) against FAOSTAT trend projections of production, by basic food; population about 23 million (2015) to 37.5 million (2050); demand outgrows production for most commodities, so net exports fall and import dependence rises. Repeats 'enough food for some 60 million people' on food energy, export-inclusive (p. 212, citing Department of Agriculture 2014; p. 219). Nutritional Production Sufficiency Index (NPSI) 5.93 (1997-1999 peak) to 4.86 (2050), maximum 6.0 (p. 219); vegetables 62% of demand in 2050, seafood under 20%, dairy net importer from 2036 (reported intake) or 2017 (dietary guide) (p. 216). No table of people covered by food group.
used_by: methods paper (section 4 (commodity balance, catalogue) and 6 (context: the nutritional sufficiency index and the food-group deficits); not a people-count comparator)
notes: Full text read (16 pp. plus a copyright page). Ten authors, confirmed from p. 211 (Ridoutt, Baird, Bastiaans, Darnell, Hendrie, Riley, Sanguansri, Syrette, Noakes, Keating); the issue number is not printed on the file. Method family: commodity balance, the same family as Foran and Poldy 2002; it reports tonnes of production against tonnes of demand and a 0-to-6 index, and has no people count of its own (the only one is the cited 60 million, food energy, export-inclusive). Earlier descriptions as a direct test of how many people supply covers (B14) are not supported. Lane: not cited. Sits with L136, L011 and B163 and the export-inclusive counts (B230); primary source of the 60 million is Department of Agriculture 2014 (see L137). The Department of Agriculture 2014 report Ridoutt cites does not contain the 60 million (B56); the figure has no traceable primary source. Underlying RIRDC reports PRJ-008806 and PRJ-009653 not seen.

title: Kastner, Ibarrola Rivas, Koch and Nonhebel 2012, PNAS 109(18), "Global changes in diets and the consequences for land requirements for food"
what_taken: Cropland needed to supply prevailing diets by world subregion 1961 to 2007, split into population, yield and diet effects; Oceania and Southern Europe above 3,000 m2 per person per year in 2005; yield gains were offset by population growth and richer diets

title: Willett et al. 2019, The Lancet 393: 447-492, "Food in the Anthropocene: the EAT-Lancet Commission on healthy diets from sustainable food systems"
what_taken: Reference healthy diet (2500 kcal/day; red meat 14 g/day) and planetary boundaries for food production for about 10 billion people (2050 model on SSP2, 9.2 billion), including cropland 13 million km2 (11-15) and no additional land; at least a 75% reduction of yield gaps; >50% cut in red meat and sugar, >100% rise in nuts, fruit, vegetables and legumes; healthy sustainable diets possible for up to 10 billion and increasingly unlikely beyond (p 453); diet change alone cuts cropland only 0-2% (p 472)
notes: Full text read 2026-11-08 (46 pp, corrected version). Method family: scenario model with a reference diet (the diet is set by judgment of the health evidence, not optimised). Lane: No (references read). Cites Peters et al. 2016 (ref 221). Australia not discussed. EAT-Lancet finds diet change alone cuts global cropland by 0 to 2% (p. 472), so it supports diet as the lever for emissions, not for cropland.

title: Giampietro and Saltelli 2014, Ecological Indicators 46: 610-621, "Footprints to nowhere"
what_taken: Critique of the ecological footprint: the protocol does not match its narrative (no external referent, world-average yields and equivalence factors, biocapacity that rises with intensification); laborious yet fragile; the deficit is set by the carbon footprint, whose assumptions are indefensible; the 50% overshoot reassures and encourages complacency; argues for several non-equivalent indicators across scales.
used_by: methods paper (section 2 and 4 (critique of the footprint family))
notes: Full text read from the archive copy. No Australian content. Does not cite Lane. The further reply (Ecological Indicators 46: 260-263) not opened.

title: Goldfinger, Wackernagel, Galli, Lazarus and Lin 2014, Ecological Indicators 46: 622-632, "Footprint facts and fallacies: a response to Giampietro and Saltelli (2014) Footprints to nowhere"
origin: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolind.2014.01.030 is the criticised paper; reply copy: https://www.footprintnetwork.org/content/uploads/2020/06/Goldfinger-Response-to-Giampetro-and-Saltelli.pdf
what_taken: Footprint network authors reply: the footprint reflects actual productivity, is not a comprehensive sustainability measure and is not prescriptive about trade; accepts limits and says refinement is a strength; argues the critique describes a version of the accounts nobody uses
notes: Full text of the author-accepted copy hosted by Global Footprint Network opened (11 pages). DOI of the reply itself not confirmed here; check against Crossref. No mention of Lane or Australia in the opening pages searched.

title: Blomqvist, Brook, Ellis, Kareiva, Nordhaus and Shellenberger 2013, PLoS Biology 11(11): e1001700, "Does the shoe fit? Real versus imagined ecological footprints"
what_taken: Argues the global footprint overshoot (1.5 Earths) comes almost wholly from the carbon footprint, which rests on one assumed forest sequestration rate (0.97 t C per ha per year); excluding carbon, biocapacity exceeds footprint by about 45% (2008); at 2.6 t C per ha per year overshoot disappears; at national scale the footprint measures self-sufficiency
used_by: methods paper (section 4 (footprint family, the critique) and 8)
notes: Full text opened (open access, 6 pages). A Brook author is at the University of Adelaide. No mention of Lane. The reply by Rees and Wackernagel (PLoS Biology 2013) was not opened.

title: Chapman and Byron 2018, Global Ecology and Conservation 13: e00365, "The flexible application of carrying capacity in ecology"
what_taken: Review of 114 ecosystem studies after Odum 1953 (from 1,170 Scopus hits; 161 human-population studies excluded): over 19 definitions of carrying capacity, most often K, the number of individuals in an area; used mostly in conservation biology, fisheries, rangeland and wildlife management and aquaculture; unclear whether static or dynamic; overshoot lowers productivity and biodiversity. Asks studies to state static or variable capacity and use plain ecological terms.
notes: Full text read (12 pp., archive copy). Method family: concept review of the ecological lineage only; it excludes human carrying capacity by design (p. 3), so it supports section 2 for the ecological lineage only. Its static-versus-variable line is quoted from Sayre 2008 (L046); cite Sayre for it. Lane: not cited.
